# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances

### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive, infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1,2]. Systemic amyloidosis involves various precursor proteins, but the two primary forms responsible for over 95% of clinical CA cases are immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [3,4]. AL amyloidosis is a clonal plasma cell disorder where unstable monoclonal light chains form amyloid fibrils [3]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis results from the dissociation of hepatic-derived transthyretin homotetramers into unstable monomers [5,6]. It is categorized into wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an age-related condition predominantly affecting older men, and hereditary or variant ATTR (ATTRv), caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [4,6]. Historically considered a rare, untreatable condition, CA is now increasingly recognized as a major contributor to heart failure, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and severe aortic stenosis [7,8].

### Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
The deposition of amyloid fibrils compromises cardiac structure and function, leading to increased ventricular wall thickness, diastolic dysfunction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy [1,8]. Patients often exhibit distinct extracardiac features that provide crucial diagnostic clues. For instance, ATTRwt is highly associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture, often preceding cardiac symptoms by years [4,9]. Conduction system disease, atrial fibrillation, and angina-like chest pain due to microvascular ischemia are also common clinical manifestations [4,8].

### Diagnostic Evaluation
The diagnostic paradigm has evolved from relying on invasive biopsy to a highly accurate non-invasive algorithm [10]. Initial screening begins with electrocardiography (ECG), which classically reveals low QRS voltages or a pseudoinfarction pattern, although left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on ECG can also occur [1,10]. Echocardiography typically demonstrates symmetric concentric left ventricular thickening, a "granular sparkling" appearance of the myocardium, and impaired longitudinal strain with characteristic "apical sparing" [11]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides superior tissue characterization, showcasing diffuse late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and expanded extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [12].

The critical step in distinguishing AL from ATTR is ruling out a monoclonal plasma cell dyscrasia [13]. This requires serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis along with a serum free light chain (sFLC) assay [13,14]. If these hematologic screens are negative, $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-pyrophosphate (PYP), $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphonnono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (DPD), or $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-hydroxymethylene diphosphonate (HMDP) scintigraphy can be used to non-invasively diagnose ATTR [13,15]. A Grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on planar/SPECT imaging, in the absence of a detectable clonal light chain, has a diagnostic specificity and positive predictive value approaching 100% for ATTR cardiomyopathy [13,15,16]. If a monoclonal protein is present or if scintigraphy is inconclusive, histological confirmation via tissue biopsy (endomyocardial or abdominal fat pad) remains necessary, demonstrating apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo red staining, with typing confirmed by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry [17,18].

### Prognosis and Staging
Accurate staging is vital for risk stratification and therapeutic planning. AL amyloidosis prognosis is determined primarily by cardiac involvement, staged using cardiac biomarkers (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP] and troponins) and the sFLC difference [19]. Untreated AL cardiac amyloidosis is highly aggressive, with historic median survival of less than six months in patients presenting with advanced heart failure [20]. Modern AL therapeutic regimens combine the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, alkylating agents, and dexamethasone with the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, which has significantly improved hematologic and clinical response rates [21].

For ATTR amyloidosis, therapies target various stages of the amyloidogenic pathway [22]. Tafamidis, a small molecule that binds to the thyroxine-binding sites of the TTR tetramer, stabilizing it and preventing dissociation, was shown in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations [22]. Genetic silencers represent another major advance: patisiran (an RNA interference therapeutic) and inotersen (an antisense oligonucleotide) inhibit the hepatic production of both wild-type and variant TTR [23,24]. Management also relies on accurate staging of ATTRwt and ATTRv, which depends on cardiac biomarkers and renal function [25,26]. Supportive care remains key, though standard heart failure therapies like beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are poorly tolerated due to restrictive physiology and fixed stroke volume; management instead focuses on cautious loop diuretic use and maintaining sinus rhythm [25,27].

### Conclusion
Historically considered a terminal disease, the paradigm has shifted toward early detection and intervention [28,29]. Clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion and understand patient experiences of diagnostic delay to optimize clinical outcomes with disease-modifying therapies [30].
